10	Eraser cloud-architecture diagrams have no explicit position control, but the layout **ranks nodes by
11	connection-statement operand order: the LEFT operand is placed earlier (further left)**, regardless of
12	arrow direction — `A < B` draws the same arrow as `B > A` but pins A left of B. Verified empirically
13	(2026-07-06, SCADA harmonization Diagram 1 v2, 4 experiments):
14	
15	- To force zone geometry `OT | iDMZ | IT`: every edge touching the middle group must be declared with
16	  the left-zone node as the left operand (`Forwarder > EMQX` for OT→iDMZ; `TimescaleDB < EMQX` for
17	  iDMZ→OT "subscribe down"; `EMQX < ModelServing` for IT→iDMZ; `EMQX > KafkaBridge` for iDMZ→IT).
18	  A single consistent assignment (left zone always on the left of the statement) yields the desired
19	  order. Declaration position in the file matters far less than operand order.
20	- Reversed dotted arrows `A <-- B` parse fine.
21	- Group-to-group edges (`ZoneA --> ZoneB: label`) are legal and render as labeled arrows between group
22	  borders — useful as semantic annotations but NOT sufficient alone to fix group order.
23	- **Export**: `export_diagram` with `format: png` fails/returns empty objects for very large canvases
24	  (~13k px wide); `format: jpeg` works. Download URLs may need a few seconds before the object is
25	  non-empty.
26	- Existing gotcha still holds: the AI edit path (`update_diagram`) reverses arrow directions — use
27	  `manually_update_diagram` with full verbatim DSL.
28

## Functional Hierarchy Levels

ISA-95 (IEC 62264) structures manufacturing IT into five levels (Level 0–4) and defines four operational domains (production, quality, maintenance, inventory). The five levels are:

- Level 0 is the physical process, Levels 1–2 cover sensing and control, Level 3 is the MES/operations layer, and Level 4 is the enterprise/ERP layer

More specifically:
- Level 0: Physical processes – Production itself: machines, raw materials, sensors and equipment

The Area contains Process Cells and Units (batch), Production Units and Units (continuous) and Production Line and Work Cells (discrete). The complete hierarchy spans from the Enterprise at the top down through the Site, Area, Production Unit, and individual equipment components.

---

# §0.1 ISA-95 / IEC 62264 — the function & data lens (the lab's spine)

## 1. Problem tie-in
Your whole thesis is *"same operational reality, described differently at every site, and it takes days to turn it into usable data."* Before you can harmonize anything you need a **shared vocabulary** for two questions every plant answers inconsistently: **"what level does this function live at?"** and **"what is a `unit` / `area` / `lot`, exactly?"** ISA-95 is that vocabulary. It's the reason your UNS topic path and your database tables can be the *same shape across four sites that each name things their own way*. No ISA-95 → no agreed skeleton to harmonize onto.

## 2. Mechanism — what it actually is
ISA-95 (US name) = **IEC 62264** (international twin — identical content). It is the **enterprise–control-system integration standard**: a *functional and data* model for how the business systems and the plant-floor systems exchange information. Hold onto one thing hard, because it's the most common mistake:

> **ISA-95 is NOT a network architecture and NOT a security standard.** It says nothing about subnets, firewalls, or zones. It only says *what functions exist and what data flows between them.* (Purdue and 62443 — coming next — are the ones about wires and security.)

It gives you **two hierarchies**:

**(a) The functional hierarchy — Levels 0–4** ("what function runs where"):

| Level | Function | Lab artifact |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| **0** | Physical process | Synthetic TEP process dynamics (your only synthetic layer) |
| **1** | Sensing & actuation | Sensors/actuators; 4–20 mA → raw counts |
| **2** | Supervisory control | PLCs / SCADA — OpenPLC (Beaumont), OPC-UA (Geismar) |
| **3** | **Manufacturing operations (MOM)** | MES / LIMS / CMMS / Quality — your OT-side transactional schemas |
| **4** | Business planning | **ERPNext** — orders, inventory, finance |

The insight that makes this a *lens*: **Level 3 is the hinge.** Above it is the business's tempo (orders, months, money); below it is the process's tempo (milliseconds, sensors, physics). Everything hard about integration happens at the L3↔L4 seam — which is exactly where your identity-reconciliation problem lives (ERP order ID ≠ MES key).

**(b) The equipment hierarchy** ("how the physical plant is organized"):

```
Enterprise → Site → Area → Production Unit → Equipment
```

This is not abstract for you — it is **literally your UNS topic path and your `asset_master` shape**:

```
lagos-chem / <site> / <area> / <production-unit> / ...
  Enterprise    Site     Area    Production Unit
 (Lagos Spec.  (Beaumont, (reaction, (a specific
  Chemicals)   Geismar…)  utilities…) reactor)
```

Note the branch choice: ISA-95 splits the bottom into **Production Unit** (continuous process — *your* branch, chemicals) vs **Line/Work Cell** (discrete manufacturing). You picked the continuous branch, and that one decision ripples all the way to why you use **lots, not batches** (the §0.1 sidebar below).

**(c) Part 2 object models** — ISA-95 also standardizes the *nouns*: **material** (definition vs lot — your N14 `material_definition`/`material_lot` tables), **equipment** (class vs instance — your P6 equipment templates), **personnel**, and **process segments**. "Class vs instance" is worth pausing on: *"Centrifugal Pump"* is a class (one template, one tag schema); *"Pump P-101 at Beaumont"* is an instance. Harmonization = every site's instances conform to shared classes.

**(d) The L3↔L4 exchange pattern — "schedule down, performance up."** This is the heartbeat of the standard:

```
   L4 (ERP)  ──── schedule / orders DOWN ────►  L3 (MOM)
   L4 (ERP)  ◄─── performance / actuals UP ───  L3 (MOM)
```

The XML binding for this conversation is **B2MML** (Business To Manufacturing Markup Language — MESA's ready-made XML schemas for ISA-95). In your lab this pattern *is* the **order-to-cash conduit C6 down** (§12 #18) and production confirmations up.

## 3. External research — how the industry states it, and where you align/diverge
The search confirms the model as taught and adds two useful nuances:

- Industry increasingly says **"MOM" (Manufacturing Operations Management)** for Level 3 rather than just "MES" — MES is the software, MOM is the ISA-95 *function*. Your L3 (MES **+** LIMS **+** CMMS **+** Quality) is precisely the MOM breadth, so your naming is more standards-correct than the common "it's the MES layer" shorthand ([Siemens](https://www.siemens.com/en-us/technology/isa-95-framework-layers/), [Symestic](https://www.symestic.com/en-us/blog/mes/isa95)).
- **"Schedule down / performance up" with monthly reconciliation** is the documented real-world pattern on large process/oil-and-gas projects — targets down from corporate, actual volumes back up through the historian, reconciled periodically ([Process Control Guide](https://processcontrolguide.com/isa-95-enterprise-integration/)). Your C6 + confirmations design mirrors this exactly.
- **Where you deliberately diverge:** classic ISA-95 integration is often *point-to-point* B2MML between an ERP and an MES. You're routing the *telemetry* side through a **UNS** instead (broker as hub). That's the modern UNS-era evolution — ISA-95 gives you the object *model* and the hierarchy; the UNS gives you the *transport*. You keep the nouns, you change the plumbing. Worth stating out loud in a presentation because purists will ask.

*(One honesty note: adoption of ISA-95 in the wild is uneven — many plants cite it but implement it partially. So "we actually modeled the equipment hierarchy end-to-end" is a genuine strength of your lab, not table stakes.)*

## 4. Gap check (light — this is a conceptual lens, not a diagram block)
Nothing to fix on the diagram yet, but two things to **verify** when we reach the blocks: (a) the UNS topic path on the diagram reads `lagos-chem/<site>/<area>/<production-unit>/…` consistently (N19), and (b) the L3 boxes (MES/LIMS/CMMS/Quality) are drawn **OT-side** — which is correct by ISA-95 function even though they feel "database-y / IT-ish." That OT-side placement is a thing people get wrong, and it's a teach-back moment when we get to Block G.

## 5. One-line teach-back (lift this into your deck)
> **"ISA-95 is the *function-and-data* standard: it gives me a 5-level functional hierarchy — physical process up to ERP — and a 5-tier equipment hierarchy — enterprise down to equipment — and my UNS topic path is literally that equipment hierarchy. It says what runs where and what data crosses the L3↔L4 seam (schedule down, performance up); it says nothing about networks or security — those are the next two lenses."**

  6. A short sidebar: ISA-88 (batch) vs ISA-106 (continuous operations) — when each

## Concepts (per component)

### E2E walkthrough §0.1 — ISA-95 / IEC 62264 (the function & data lens; the lab's spine)

*Captured 2026-07-11 during the Diagram 1 v2 walkthrough opener (E2E_WALKTHROUGH.md §0.1).*

**What it is / isn't.** ISA-95 (US) = IEC 62264 (international twin, identical content) is the
**enterprise–control-system integration standard**: a *functional and data* model for how business
systems and plant-floor systems exchange information. **It is NOT a network architecture and NOT a
security standard** — that is the single most common misconception. Networks = Purdue; security =
IEC 62443. ISA-95 only says *what functions exist and what data flows between them.*

**Two hierarchies:**
1. **Functional hierarchy (Levels 0–4)** — L0 physical process · L1 sensing/actuation · L2 supervisory
   control · **L3 Manufacturing Operations Management (MOM)** — MES/LIMS/CMMS/Quality · L4 business
   planning (ERP). *Level 3 is the hinge*: business tempo above (orders, months, money), process tempo
   below (ms, sensors, physics). Every hard integration problem lives at the L3↔L4 seam — which is
   exactly where identity reconciliation bites (ERP order ID ≠ MES key).
2. **Equipment hierarchy** — `Enterprise → Site → Area → Production Unit → Equipment`. This *is* the
   lab's UNS topic path `lagos-chem/<site>/<area>/<production-unit>/…` (§14 N19) and the `asset_master`
   shape. ISA-95 splits the bottom into **Production Unit** (continuous — the lab's branch) vs
   **Line/Work Cell** (discrete) vs **Process Cell/Unit** (batch).

**Part 2 object models** (the standardized nouns): **material** (definition vs lot → N14
`material_definition`/`material_lot`), **equipment** (class vs instance → P6 templates; *"Centrifugal
Pump"* = class, *"P-101 at Beaumont"* = instance — harmonization = every site's instances conform to
shared classes), **personnel**, **process segments**.

**L3↔L4 exchange pattern — "schedule down, performance up."** Orders/targets flow down, actuals/
performance flow up, reconciled periodically. XML binding = **B2MML** (MESA's ready-made ISA-95 XML
schemas; the model can also be JSON / OPC-UA information models). In the lab this pattern *is* the
order-to-cash conduit **C6 down** + production confirmations up (§12 #18).

**Where the lab aligns / diverges (web-checked):** industry increasingly says **"MOM"** for L3, not
just "MES" (MES is the software, MOM is the ISA-95 function) — the lab's L3 breadth
(MES+LIMS+CMMS+Quality) is the standards-correct MOM scope. "Schedule down/performance up with periodic
reconciliation" is the documented real-world process/O&G pattern. **Deliberate divergence:** classic
ISA-95 integration is point-to-point B2MML (ERP↔MES); the lab keeps the ISA-95 *object model + hierarchy*
but routes telemetry through a **UNS** (broker-as-hub) instead — same nouns, modern plumbing. Adoption
in the wild is uneven/partial, so "we modeled the equipment hierarchy end-to-end" is a genuine strength.

**Sidebar — ISA-88 vs ISA-106:** because LSC is a *continuous* process, production is modeled as
**lots** (ISA-106 continuous ops), not **batches** (ISA-88) → table is `production_lot`, not `batch`
(§14 N13).

**Teach-back:** *"ISA-95 is the function-and-data standard: a 5-level functional hierarchy (physical
process → ERP) and a 5-tier equipment hierarchy (enterprise → equipment); my UNS topic path IS that
equipment hierarchy. It says what runs where and what crosses the L3↔L4 seam (schedule down,
performance up) — nothing about networks or security; those are Purdue and 62443."*

**Sources:** [Siemens ISA-95 framework](https://www.siemens.com/en-us/technology/isa-95-framework-layers/) ·
[Symestic — ISA-95 for MES/ERP](https://www.symestic.com/en-us/blog/mes/isa95) ·
[Process Control Guide — ISA-95 enterprise integration](https://processcontrolguide.com/isa-95-enterprise-integration/) ·
[ISA.org — ISA-95 standard](https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-95-standard).
